title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
This is the final page of E297. It does two things.

(1) The scholium closes the paper by stressing what the new analytic (Lagrangian, δ-) method adds. Integration by parts produces 'partes absolutae' (boundary terms). These terms fix the integration constants that the older geometric method of the Methodus inveniendi (1744) left undetermined. Euler's example is the brachistochrone from a given point to a given line or curve, rather than to a given point. Making the boundary terms vanish at the free end yields the condition that the brachistochrone must cut the given curve at right angles. In modern terms this is the natural boundary / transversality condition. For the functional T = ∫ sqrt(1+y'^2)/sqrt(y) dx, transversality with a curve reduces to orthogonality, because the integrand has the form f(x,y)·sqrt(1+y'^2).

(2) Euler then proposes, 'for examination by analysts', a theorem. Let Z = Z(x, y, p, q, r, …) with p = y', q = y'', … and dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + …. Form V = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + …, with dx held constant. Then Z dx is an exact differential (Z is a total derivative dW/dx of some function of x, y, y', …) if V = 0, and not if V ≠ 0. V is exactly the Euler–Lagrange expression of ∫Z dx. In modern language: the Euler operator E(Z) vanishes identically iff Z = D_x W.

Necessity follows, as Euler says, 'from the principles laid down': if Z = D_x W, then ∫Z dx depends only on boundary data, so its first variation has no interior part and V ≡ 0. Sufficiency is the nontrivial direction. Euler announces it without proof here.
errors: The statement needs V to vanish identically, as a formal identity in x, y, p, q, … for all functions y. Merely V = 0 as a differential equation is not enough. Euler's wording 'si reperiatur nihilo aequalis' leaves this implicit.
No proof is given, either of sufficiency or of the regularity and domain assumptions (local exactness only). This is a gap rather than an error; the claim is correct locally.

ideas.what: Free-endpoint brachistochrone: the boundary terms of the variation force the curve to meet the given terminal curve orthogonally.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli (orthogonality for brachistochrone to a line, 1697); general analytic treatment Lagrange 1760s and Euler E296/E297
ideas.where_published: E296 'Elementa calculi variationum', E297 (Novi Comm. Petrop. 10, 1766); later Institutiones calculi integralis vol. 3 appendix

ideas.what: Criterion that Z(x, y, y', …) dx is an exact differential iff its Euler–Lagrange expression vanishes identically.
ideas.modern_name: Exactness theorem for the Euler operator (kernel of the Euler operator = total divergences); first step of the variational bicomplex
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (stated 1766 in E297); proofs and discussion by Condorcet and Lagrange; modern form via Volterra, Helmholtz-type results, Olver, Anderson
ideas.where_published: E297 (this page); taken up again in Euler's later integrability papers and Inst. calc. int.; discussed by Engelsman and Fraser in histories of the calculus of variations

deep.surprise_reason: Both the transversality example and the integrability theorem are well-known parts of E297. Historians of the calculus of variations, notably Engelsman and Fraser, explicitly credit Euler with the integrability criterion stated here. Nothing appears overlooked.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'grue' continues 'congrue' from the previous page; this is correct, not an error.
'a dato, puncto' — the comma placement follows the print; the reading is fine.
The facing page 135 is the title page of E298 'De insigni promotione methodi tangentium inversae', not part of E297.
